questions.question: What is a ResultSet in JDBC and how do you iterate it?
questions.title: JDBC ResultSet — Iterating Query Results
questions.direct_answer: A **ResultSet** is a **cursor** over the rows returned by a query. It starts positioned **before the first row**; you call **`next()`** to advance (it returns `false` when rows run out) and `getXxx("col")` to read columns. It's forward-only by default and must be closed.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you know ResultSet is a cursor and the next()/getXxx iteration loop.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Reading a column before calling next(), or assuming it's a loaded list.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Note the cursor starts before row 1 and ResultSet is forward-only by default.

sections.title: Quick revision
sections.content:
- **ResultSet** is a cursor over query rows.
- **Starts before the first row** — call `next()` before reading.
- **`next()`** advances and returns `false` when done.
- **Read** with `getXxx` by column name or 1-based index.
- **Forward-only by default**; close it (try-with-resources).

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content: A ResultSet is a cursor over the rows that a query returns. It's important to understand it's a cursor, not a fully loaded list in memory; it points at one row at a time. The cursor starts positioned before the first row, which is the key detail people forget. So to read data, you first call next, which moves the cursor to the next row and returns true if there's a row there, or false when you've run off the end. That's why the standard pattern is a while loop on rs dot next. Inside the loop, you read each column with the typed getters, like getInt and getString, and you can read either by column name, which is more readable, or by a one-based column index. By default a ResultSet is forward-only, meaning you iterate through it once from start to finish, and it's tied to the Statement and Connection that produced it, so once those are closed the ResultSet is invalid. That's why you close it when you're done, ideally with try-with-resources. The mistakes to avoid are trying to read a column before calling next, since the cursor starts before the first row, treating the ResultSet like a reusable list, and using zero-based column indices when they're actually one-based.

sections.title: The cursor moves one row at a time
sections.content:
A `ResultSet` represents the rows produced by a statement and maintains a cursor position. The cursor begins before row one. Each successful call to `next()` moves it forward and makes that row available through getters such as `getLong`, `getString`, or `getObject`. When `next()` returns `false`, no rows remain.

For example, `while (rs.next())` can map every row into a domain object using column labels. SQL `NULL` needs care: primitive getters return a default primitive value, so call `wasNull()` when zero or false could be meaningful, or use a suitable object getter. A result set belongs to its statement and connection, so all three should be closed with try-with-resources and not returned outside that scope.

sections.title: ResultSet at a Glance
sections.content:
blue|What|~a cursor|over query rows|not a loaded list|tied to its Statement
emerald|Iterate|~next() loop|starts before row 1|next() returns true/false|getXxx to read
amber|Read columns|~by name or index|getString("name")|getInt(1)|1-based index
rose|Default|~forward-only|read once|close when done|try-with-resources

sections.title: Iterating a ResultSet
Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Reading before `next()`**: the cursor starts before the first row — always call `next()` first.
- **Treating it as a list**: it's a forward cursor, read once.
- **Using it after closing the Statement/Connection**: the ResultSet becomes invalid.
- **0-based column index**: indices are 1-based (`getInt(1)`).

speakable_v2.standard_example: Java 17 app querying an orders table over JDBC
speakable_v2.hook: A ResultSet doesn't hand you a list. It's a cursor that sits before row one until you call next.

beats.text: A ResultSet is a cursor over the rows a query returns. It's not a list in memory. It points at one row at a time. The cursor starts before the first row. So you call next to move forward. That call returns true when a row's there. It returns false once the rows run out.
Why a cursor and not a list? Big queries can return millions of rows. Loading them all at once would blow up memory. A cursor streams rows one by one. So your app stays light even on huge tables.

items: Before-first position. The cursor sits here at the start. Read now and you'll get nothing back.
The next call moves the cursor ahead by one row. It returns true when that row's there.
Typed getters by name like getInt of id stay readable as columns grow.
Typed getters by index, like the first column, run a hair faster but break when column order shifts.
After-last position. Here next returns false and the loop stops.

beats.text: Say we fetch orders. executeQuery hands back a ResultSet. The while loop calls next. The first call lands on row one and returns true. getLong of id reads that column. When rows run out, next returns false and the loop ends. Here's the non-obvious part. The driver pulls rows in batches using a fetch size, not one per trip.

items: Reading a column before the first next call. The cursor's still before row one, so it throws.
Trusting a column index when SELECT star order can change. Column names stay safer.

speakable_v2.cap: So treat a ResultSet as a forward cursor. Call next before each read, and close it when you're done.

questions.question: How do you check for NULL values when reading from a ResultSet?
questions.title: Checking NULL Values in JDBC ResultSet
questions.direct_answer: Primitive-style getters such as getInt and getLong return 0 when the SQL value is NULL, so call wasNull immediately after that getter to distinguish NULL from a real zero. getObject can return Java null, and modern JDBC can request a wrapper/type such as getObject(column, Integer.class) when supported. Reference getters such as getString normally return null for SQL NULL.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you know primitive getters return 0 for NULL and how to detect it.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Treating a returned 0/false as a real value when the column was NULL.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Use wasNull() immediately after the read, or getObject for nullable columns.

sections.title: Reading SQL NULL from ResultSet
sections.content:
SQL NULL and Java defaults are different. Mapping NULL to 0 can incorrectly turn 'not measured' into a valid measurement. Row-mapping code should reflect the column's nullability and domain meaning.

wasNull is easy to misuse because any later getter changes which column it describes. A reusable RowMapper plus tests containing both NULL and zero catches the mistake.

**Example.** Integer age = rs.getObject("age", Integer.class) preserves SQL NULL as Java null. With int age = rs.getInt("age"), both NULL and numeric zero return 0, so rs.wasNull() immediately after that getter distinguishes them.

sections.title: Quick revision
content: wasNull refers to the value read by the most recent getter.
Call it immediately before another getXxx changes that state.
Use wrapper/object mappings when nullability belongs in the Java model.
Do not convert missing numeric values to zero unless that is the business rule.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
int score = rs.getInt("score"); boolean missing = rs.wasNull(); is the classic pattern. If score can be absent, mapping it directly to primitive int loses information; use Integer and getObject where the driver supports the requested conversion. For String name = rs.getString("name"), a SQL NULL becomes Java null, so wasNull is usually unnecessary for that getter.

For example, getInt("discount") returns 0 for both SQL NULL and zero. Calling wasNull() immediately afterward, or using getObject with Integer, preserves the difference.

sections.title: NULL in ResultSet at a Glance
sections.content:
rose|Primitive getters|~0 for NULL|getInt -> 0|getBoolean -> false|ambiguous
blue|wasNull()|~the check|call right after getter|true if last read was NULL|positional
emerald|getObject|~returns null|Integer / null|clean for nullable cols|preferred
amber|String getters|~already null|getString -> null|no wasNull needed|

sections.title: Ambiguous: 0 might be a real value or NULL
Clear: use wasNull() or getObject
Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Trusting a returned 0/false**: it may be a NULL, not a real value.
- **Calling `wasNull()` too late**: it refers to the *last* column read — call it right after.
- **Mapping nullable columns to primitives**: use wrappers/`getObject`.
- **Forgetting `getString` returns null**: object getters already handle NULL.

seo.metaDescription: Interview answer for How do you check for NULL values when reading from a ResultSet? with a clear explanation, practical example, common mistakes, and follow-up questions.

speakable_v2.standard_example: Java 17 app querying an orders table over JDBC
speakable_v2.hook: getInt gives back zero for a NULL column. So is it a real zero, or just missing? On its own, that zero won't tell you.

beats.text: When a column is NULL, the getter's result depends on its return type. Object getters like getString hand back Java null. Primitive getters like getInt hand back zero, and getBoolean hands back false. To catch the difference, call wasNull right after a primitive getter.
Why the gap? Java primitives can't hold null. So a primitive getter has to return some default. JDBC picks zero or false, then offers wasNull as the real signal.

items: Object getters like getString and getObject. They return Java null for a NULL, so a null check just works.
Primitive getters like getInt and getDouble. They return zero or false for a NULL, which stays ambiguous.
wasNull. It reports true when the last column read was NULL. Call it right after the getter.
getObject with a cast. It returns null directly, so you skip the wasNull dance for nullable numbers.

beats.text: Picture a nullable discount column on the orders table. You read int discount with getInt. Then you call wasNull. If it's true, the discount wasn't set. If it's false, the real value's zero or more. Here's the non-obvious part. A cleaner route reads Integer discount from getObject. That returns null straight away, with no wasNull needed.

items: Reading another column between getInt and wasNull. wasNull tracks the last read, so order matters.
Mapping a nullable total to a primitive. Then zero for no charge looks the same as NULL.

speakable_v2.cap: So never map a nullable column to a primitive blindly. Check wasNull right after, or just use getObject.

questions.question: How do you map ResultSet rows to Java objects in JDBC?
questions.title: Mapping ResultSet to Java Objects in JDBC
questions.direct_answer: ResultSet mapping reads each row's columns, handles SQL nulls and type conversion, and constructs a Java DTO/domain value. Keep the mapping in a focused function or RowMapper so query aliases and object construction stay consistent. Spring JdbcTemplate calls a RowMapper once per row and manages iteration/resource cleanup around it.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you can convert rows into domain objects cleanly.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Inlining mapping everywhere, duplicating column reads and bugs.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Extract a RowMapper; mention Spring JdbcTemplate uses exactly this abstraction.

sections.title: Mapping ResultSet Rows to Java Values
sections.content:
Time zones and numeric precision need special attention. BigDecimal preserves decimal values better than double for money. getObject with LocalDate/LocalDateTime/OffsetDateTime depends on JDBC driver support and column semantics.

A mapper should not execute another query for each row; that recreates N+1 in mapping code. Fetch the required set or collect keys for one bulk query. Keep business decisions outside the low-level row conversion when possible.

sections.title: Quick revision
content: Alias calculated/joined columns to stable names.
Use appropriate getters/getObject and handle nullable columns deliberately.
Construct immutable DTOs where possible instead of partially initialized objects.
Test joins, duplicate column names, NULL, timestamps, decimals, and empty results.

sections.title: Interview answer
Row Mapping at a Glance
sections.content:
blue|Pattern|~loop + build|next() per row|read columns|construct object
emerald|RowMapper|~ResultSet -> T|one place for mapping|reusable|testable
amber|Collect|~into a List|add per row|return list|or Optional for one
rose|Spring|~same idea|JdbcTemplate RowMapper|query(sql, mapper)|less boilerplate

sections.title: Mapping Recipe
sections.content:
| Step | Action |
|---|---|
| 1 | run query → `ResultSet` |
| 2 | `while (rs.next())` |
| 3 | read columns, build object |
| 4 | add to `List<T>`, return |

sections.title: A reusable RowMapper
Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Inlining mapping everywhere**: duplicates column reads; extract a RowMapper.
- **Column name typos**: a wrong name throws at runtime — keep mapping centralized.
- **Ignoring NULLs**: use `getObject`/`wasNull` for nullable columns.
- **Building objects before `next()`**: read only after advancing the cursor.

seo.metaTitle: Mapping ResultSet to Java Objects in JDBC — java backend interview question | InterviewExplainer
seo.metaDescription: Interview answer for How do you map ResultSet rows to Java objects in JDBC? with a clear explanation, practical example, common mistakes, and follow-up questions.

speakable_v2.standard_example: Java 17 app querying an orders table over JDBC
speakable_v2.hook: Stop hand-copying columns in every query. A RowMapper turns one row into one object, in a single reusable spot.

beats.text: Mapping a ResultSet to objects means reading each column and filling a Java object. Raw JDBC makes you write that by hand. Spring's JdbcTemplate takes a RowMapper lambda instead. JPA does it for you from entity annotations.
Why bother with mappers? JDBC hands you flat rows and columns. Your code wants real objects. The mapping bridges those two worlds. It's needed work, but it gets repetitive fast.

items: Manual JDBC. You loop with next, build an object per row, and add it to a list. Verbose but clear.
JdbcTemplate RowMapper. You pass a lambda, and it handles the loop and resource cleanup for you.
JPA or Hibernate. You annotate fields, and the ORM maps columns to fields with zero hand code.

beats.text: Take the orders table. Raw JDBC builds a new Order per row. It calls getLong of id and getBigDecimal of total, then adds to a list. JdbcTemplate shrinks that to one query call with a small lambda. Here's the non-obvious part. JdbcTemplate's ColumnMapRowMapper reads ResultSetMetaData to build a generic map per row.

items: Hardcoding column indexes in manual mapping. A SELECT star reorder then corrupts every object quietly.
Reusing one mutable object across the loop. Every list entry ends up pointing at the same row.

speakable_v2.cap: So raw mapping's verbose, RowMapper's cleaner, and JPA's cleanest. Match the tool to your query.

questions.question: What happens if you do not close a ResultSet in JDBC?
questions.title: Consequences of Not Closing ResultSet in JDBC
questions.direct_answer: A ResultSet can retain driver, statement, connection, memory, network, or database cursor resources until it is closed. Exact resources depend on the driver and result mode; it is not guaranteed that every ResultSet holds a server cursor. Failing to close results/statements can delay returning a pooled connection and eventually cause resource exhaustion. Use try-with-resources.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you know unclosed ResultSets leak cursors and the try-with-resources fix.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Relying on Statement/Connection close or GC to clean up the ResultSet.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Note closing the Statement closes its ResultSet, but explicit try-with-resources is clearest.

sections.title: Why ResultSet Must Be Closed
sections.content:
Some frameworks manage the JDBC lifecycle around callbacks, so application code should follow that ownership contract rather than closing framework-managed resources unexpectedly. In raw JDBC, the caller that creates the result normally closes it.

Monitor open connections, active statements, and database cursor/session counts when diagnosing leaks. A slow consumer can look like a leak even when close eventually happens.

sections.title: Quick revision
content: Close ResultSet promptly after reading the rows.
Closing its Statement or Connection also closes dependent results under JDBC rules, but explicit nested scopes show ownership.
Streaming/fetch-size modes can hold database resources for longer.
Pool exhaustion, cursor limits, or memory pressure are possible symptoms—not one guaranteed failure.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content: A query that streams millions of rows may keep the statement and connection busy until the result is consumed or closed. A small fully buffered result may not hold a server-side cursor, but its JDBC objects still need deterministic cleanup. Nest ResultSet and PreparedStatement inside the Connection's try-with-resources block so exceptions close them in reverse order.

sections.title: Unclosed ResultSet at a Glance
sections.content:
rose|Leak|~holds resources|DB cursor + buffers|not released|accumulates
blue|Symptom|~under load|open-cursor limit hit|errors/hangs|hard to spot in tests
amber|GC not enough|~non-deterministic|don't rely on it|close explicitly|
emerald|Fix|~try-with-resources|auto-close|even on exception|reverse order

sections.title: Leak-prone: ResultSet not closed on error
Safe: try-with-resources closes the ResultSet

seo.metaTitle: Consequences of Not Closing ResultSet in JDBC — java backend interview question | InterviewExplainer
seo.metaDescription: Interview answer for What happens if you do not close a ResultSet in JDBC? with a clear explanation, practical example, common mistakes, and follow-up questions.

speakable_v2.standard_example: Java 17 app querying an orders table over JDBC
speakable_v2.hook: An unclosed ResultSet quietly pins a database cursor. Stack up enough and the cursor limit hits, and queries start failing.

beats.text: Every open ResultSet holds a server-side cursor. That cursor eats database memory and counts toward the server's open-cursor limit. Skip the close and it lingers. It stays open until the connection closes or the database times it out.
Why does closing matter so much? A ResultSet isn't just a Java object. It maps to a live cursor the database server tracks. Closing tells that server to free the cursor's resources right away.

items: Unclosed ResultSet. The server cursor stays open and keeps eating memory on the database.
Cursor limit hit. Oracle throws ORA-01000 for too many open cursors, and MySQL caps it too.
Implicit close chain. Closing a Statement closes its ResultSets, but leaning on that stays risky.
try-with-resources. It closes the ResultSet, then the Statement, in reverse order on its own.

beats.text: Say a method fetches orders but an exception jumps out before the close. That server cursor stays open. Repeat it under load and a hundred leaked cursors pile up. Soon you trip a max-open-cursors error. Here's the non-obvious part. try-with-resources on the ResultSet frees the cursor no matter what exception flies.

items: Trusting Connection close to clean up. It works late, but the cursor sits open the whole time.
Assuming JPA makes this moot. Hibernate opens JDBC result sets too, and bad lazy loading leaves them open.

speakable_v2.cap: So always close result sets on purpose. try-with-resources is the safest one-line way to guarantee it.
